practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following biomes has the highest annual rainfall?
A) Tropical rainforest
B) Hot desert
C) Tundra
D) Temperate grassland
practice_questions.marks: A) Tropical rainforest. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'biome'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A large-scale ecosystem found around the world that shares similar climate, plants and animals, such as tropical rainforest or tundra.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'A type of ecosystem like rainforest or desert.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the global distribution of hot deserts.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: located around 30°N and 30°S latitude; on the western sides of continents; named examples — Sahara (North Africa), Arabian, Australian, Atacama (South America), Sonoran (North America). Mastering: latitude pattern + 2 named examples. [3]

practice_questions.text: Explain why tropical rainforests are found near the equator.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: equator receives the most direct and intense sunlight, so air heats and rises (Hadley cell rising arm); rising air cools, condenses and produces year-round heavy rainfall; constant high temperatures (25–28°C) plus 2,000+ mm rainfall create perfect conditions for evergreen forest; high biodiversity follows. Mastering: full chain from sunlight → circulation → rainfall → vegetation. [4]

practice_questions.text: A tropical rainforest receives 2,400 mm of rainfall a year. Calculate the average monthly rainfall. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 2,400 ÷ 12 = 200 mm/month. Working clear, units. [4]
Secure: 200 mm with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error. [2]
Emerging: tries division. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine how local factors modify the broad pattern of biomes shaped by global climate.
(8 marks)
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: altitude — Mount Kilimanjaro shows tropical/alpine/icecap zones at one location; soil — rainforest grows on poor soils with rapid nutrient cycling; drainage — wetlands form even in dry regions; rock type — granite gives acidic moorland; ocean currents — Atacama desert exists on a tropical coast because cold Humboldt current suppresses rainfall. Conclusion: latitude/circulation set the broad pattern but local factors create regional and altitudinal variations. Mastering (7–8): 3+ factors with named examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an igneous rock that forms an upland UK landscape?
A) Chalk in the South Downs
B) Granite in the Cairngorms
C) Clay in the London Basin
D) Coal in South Wales
practice_questions.marks: B) Granite in the Cairngorms. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'glacial till'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A mixture of clay, sand and stones deposited directly by a glacier, often forming gently rolling hills or fertile lowland soils.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Material left behind by a glacier.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the contrast between upland and lowland landscapes in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Uplands (north and west) are areas of high relief, often above 300 m, with mountains, rocky outcrops and U-shaped valleys.
• Lowlands (south and east) sit below 200 m, with gentle slopes, wide plains and rolling chalk and clay hills.
• The Tees-Exe Line broadly separates the two zones.
• Uplands have a wetter, cooler climate; lowlands are drier and warmer.
Mastering: clear contrast covering both relief and location. [3]
Secure: contrast given without specifics. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how geology and past glaciation have helped to create the UK's distinctive landscapes.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Geology: hard igneous and metamorphic rocks (granite Cairngorms, slate Snowdonia) resist erosion and stand high; softer sedimentary rocks (chalk South Downs, clay London Basin) are worn down faster and form lowlands.
• Glaciation: Devensian ice up to a kilometre thick carved U-shaped valleys, cirques and ribbon lakes such as Wast Water; ice deposited fertile till across East Anglia and the Vale of York.
• Post-glacial: weathering and mass movement continue to modify mountain landscapes; misfit streams flow in oversized valleys.
Mastering: both geology and glaciation linked to specific landscapes. [4]
Secure: factors named with limited explanation. [2-3]

practice_questions.text: The Lake District attracts about 18 million visitors a year. If the average visitor stay is 2.5 days, how many visitor-days does the park host annually? Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 18,000,000 × 2.5 = 45,000,000 visitor-days per year. Working clearly shown, units stated. [4]
Secure: correct answer with method. [3]
Developing: correct method with arithmetic slip. [2]
Emerging: answer only without working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Assess the relative importance of physical and human factors in shaping UK landscapes.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Physical: rock type and structure (igneous granite forming Dartmoor, chalk forming the South Downs); past tectonic activity raising upland Britain; glaciation carving valleys, lakes and cirques in the Lake District and Snowdonia; deposition of fertile till across East Anglia.
• Post-glacial physical: weathering, mass movement and rivers continue to shape relief.
• Human: deforestation reducing UK forest cover to about 13%; lowland farming creating hedged field patterns; upland sheep grazing keeping moors open; mining (slate quarries in Snowdonia, china clay in Cornwall) leaving spoil heaps.
• Settlement and urbanisation: cities like London, Manchester and Birmingham covering natural surfaces; transport networks reshaping rural areas.
• Conclusion: physical processes set the stage by creating relief and rock; humans then heavily modified what was there. Almost no UK landscape is genuinely 'natural'.
Mastering (7–8): physical and human factors with named examples and clear linkage.
Secure (5–6): both factors covered with examples.
Developing (3–4): one factor covered well.
Emerging (1–2): vague description with no examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Hadley cell?
A) A loop of moving air between 30° and 60° latitude
B) A loop of moving air between the equator and 30° latitude
C) A current of warm water in the Atlantic Ocean
D) A weather front that brings rain to the UK
practice_questions.marks: B) A loop of moving air between the equator and 30° latitude. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'atmospheric pressure'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The weight or force of air pressing down on the Earth's surface, measured in millibars or hectopascals.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'The weight of air pressing on the surface.' [1 mark]
Developing/Emerging: vague reference to weather or temperature without naming weight or air column. [0 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern of high-pressure and low-pressure zones.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Low pressure at the equator (rising air, heavy rainfall, equatorial belt of forests).
• High pressure at around 30°N and 30°S (sinking air, location of major deserts).
• Low pressure again at 60° latitude (rising air, temperate rainfall belt).
• High pressure over the poles (sinking cold dry air).
Mastering: clearly described locations of all three pressure types. [3]
Secure: two correctly described. [2]
Developing: one correct point. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how global atmospheric circulation creates the world's great deserts.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Air rises at the equator, having been heated by intense sunlight (point 1).
• At altitude it cools, releasing moisture as rainfall, then travels polewards.
• At around 30° latitude this dry air sinks back to the surface (point 2).
• Sinking air warms by compression, can hold more moisture, so very little rainfall reaches the surface — creating arid zones such as the Sahara, Arabian and Atacama deserts.
Mastering: full chain of reasoning linking sinking air → high pressure → aridity → named desert. [4]
Secure: cause–effect chain identifying sinking air and dry conditions. [3]
Developing: identifies sinking air at 30° but no full chain. [2]
Emerging: simple statement that 30° is dry. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A climate graph shows monthly rainfall in a tropical location: 200, 220, 210, 195, 205, 215, 225, 230, 220, 215, 210, 200 (mm).
Calculate the mean monthly rainfall. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: total = 2,545 mm; mean = 2,545 ÷ 12 = 212.08 mm (accept 212.1 or 212). Working shown. [4]
Secure: correct method and correct arithmetic to 211–213 with units. [3]
Developing: correct method but arithmetic error of <±5 mm or units missing. [2]
Emerging: attempts addition or division but does not complete or shows working error. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine how global atmospheric circulation influences the global pattern of arid and high-rainfall areas.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Tropical rainforests cluster on the equator because rising Hadley-cell air produces year-round heavy rainfall, ideal for dense vegetation.
• Deserts cluster at ~30° latitude because Hadley-cell air sinks, creating high pressure and aridity (Sahara, Arabian, Australian).
• Temperate biomes occur at 50–60° latitude where the Ferrel cell rises, generating regular but moderate rainfall (UK deciduous forest, grassland).
• Polar biomes (tundra) lie under the Polar cell where cold sinking air gives very low precipitation and freezing temperatures.
• Ocean currents modify biomes locally — e.g. North Atlantic Drift gives north-west Europe temperate climate further north than expected.
Mastering (7–8): sustained, well-evidenced argument linking circulation to multiple biomes with specific examples and clear chains of reasoning.
Secure (5–6): clear argument and at least two named biomes linked to circulation cells.
Developing (3–4): basic links between cells and rainfall, limited examples.
Emerging (1–2): simple statements without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a natural cause of climate change?
A) Volcanic activity
B) Burning of coal in power stations
C) Variations in solar output
D) Asteroid impacts
practice_questions.marks: B) Burning of coal in power stations. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two examples of evidence used to reconstruct past climate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: any two of: ice cores; tree rings; historical sources; pollen analysis; coral records. [2 marks]
Secure: one valid example. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the trend in atmospheric CO₂ concentration since 1750.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include: rise from ~280 ppm (1750) to over 420 ppm today; rate steepening since 1950; today's level is highest in 800,000 years of ice-core data. Mastering: trend, figures and rate-of-change all addressed. [3]
Secure: trend with one figure. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activities have caused recent climate change.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: burning fossil fuels releases CO₂; deforestation removes carbon-absorbing trees; cattle and rice paddies release methane; cement manufacture releases CO₂; these enhance the greenhouse effect, trapping more heat. Mastering: causal chain activity → emissions → enhanced greenhouse effect → warming. [4]

practice_questions.text: Atmospheric CO₂ was 280 ppm in 1750 and 420 ppm in 2024. Calculate the percentage increase. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = 140; (140 ÷ 280) × 100 = 50%. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 50% with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error. [2]
Emerging: subtraction only. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the reasons why projections of future climate change have a wide range of possible outcomes.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: future emissions depend on policy and technology choices; climate feedbacks (permafrost methane, albedo) amplify uncertainty; IPCC pathways span 1.5°C–4.4°C; uncertain ice-sheet behaviour; natural variability. Mastering (7–8): three uncertainty sources with named pathways and feedbacks. Secure (5–6): two sources. Developing (3–4): acknowledges uncertainty. Emerging (1–2): vague.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a depositional landform?
A) An arch
B) A stack
C) A spit
D) A wave-cut platform
practice_questions.marks: C) A spit. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'longshore drift'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The zigzag movement of sediment along a coastline, caused by waves approaching the shore at an angle and the backwash returning straight down the slope.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'When sand and pebbles move along a beach.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of destructive waves.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• High and steep wave profile.
• High frequency — about 10 to 14 waves per minute.
• Stronger backwash than swash, which pulls material off the beach.
• Tend to erode rather than build beaches.
Mastering: two characteristics with detail. [3]
Secure: two characteristics named. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a stack forms on a coast of erosion.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A weakness (joint or fault) in a headland is widened by hydraulic action and abrasion.
• Continuous erosion enlarges the weakness into a cave.
• Two caves on opposite sides of the headland meet, forming an arch.
• The arch is undercut by erosion and weakened by sub-aerial processes.
• Eventually the roof collapses, leaving an isolated pillar — a stack — separated from the headland.
• Named example: Old Harry Rocks, Dorset; Flamborough Head, Yorkshire.
Mastering: process linked stage-by-stage with named example. [4]
Secure: stages mentioned without full chain. [2-3]

practice_questions.text: The Holderness coast retreats at about 2 m per year. How many metres of cliff would be lost over a 35-year period? Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 2 × 35 = 70 metres of cliff retreat over 35 years. Working clearly shown, units stated. [4]
Secure: correct answer with method. [3]
Developing: correct method with arithmetic slip. [2]
Emerging: answer only without working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Assess the relative importance of marine, sub-aerial and human processes in shaping coastal landscapes in the UK.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Marine: destructive waves erode through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution; constructive waves build beaches; longshore drift moves sediment along the coast.
• Sub-aerial: freeze-thaw weathering opens cracks; mass movement (slumping, rockfall) drags material down cliffs after rain.
• Geology: discordant coasts at Studland produce headlands and bays; concordant coasts at Lulworth produce coves once the front band is breached.
• Human: hard engineering (sea walls, groynes) protects some coasts but starves others of sediment downdrift; tourism creates footpath erosion; reclamation of marshland alters the natural sediment system.
• Specific case: Holderness coast retreating 2 m a year; eroded till feeds Spurn Head; sea defences at Mappleton intercept sediment, starving the coast further south.
• Conclusion: coastal landforms are the result of marine and sub-aerial processes acting on the local geology, with human activity often modifying or accelerating natural patterns.
Mastering (7–8): all three sets of processes covered with named examples and clear linkage.
Secure (5–6): two sets of processes with examples.
Developing (3–4): one process explored well.
Emerging (1–2): vague description with no examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a driver of rising demand on the biosphere?
A) Population growth
B) Urbanisation
C) Falling life expectancy
D) Industrialisation
practice_questions.marks: C) Falling life expectancy. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'water stress'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A situation where demand for water in a region exceeds the amount available, even when rainfall may be adequate, often caused by overuse of groundwater or irrigation.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'When there isn't enough water to meet demand.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways rising affluence increases pressure on the biosphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Wealthier people eat more meat and dairy, which use much more land and water per calorie than grain crops.
• Higher incomes mean more cars, larger homes, air conditioning and frequent flying — all raising energy and resource use.
• Wealthier consumers replace electronics and clothes more often, raising demand for minerals and water.
Mastering: two clear ways with development and named example (e.g. Chinese meat consumption rising from 13 kg to 60 kg per capita). [3]
Secure: two ways named with brief explanation. [2]
Developing: one way named, weak development. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how Malthus and Boserup differ in their views on population and resources.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Malthus (1798) argued population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, so population must outrun food, leading to famine, disease or war (positive checks).
• Boserup (1965) argued the opposite — population pressure drives innovation: new farming methods and technologies raise output to match demand.
• Malthus is essentially pessimistic; Boserup essentially optimistic.
• Both can be illustrated — Malthus through famines in the Sahel, Boserup through the Green Revolution.
Mastering: clear contrast between both theories with named example for each. [4]
Secure: both theories accurately stated with one example. [3]

practice_questions.text: World population was around 2.5 billion in 1950 and is projected to peak at about 10 billion by 2080. Calculate the percentage increase in population from 1950 to the projected peak. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = 10 − 2.5 = 7.5 billion; percentage increase = (7.5 ÷ 2.5) × 100 = 300%. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 300% with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the view that Boserup's theory better explains today's relationship between population and resources than Malthus's theory.
(8 marks)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Arguments supporting Boserup:
• Global food output has grown faster than population since 1960, thanks to the Green Revolution, GM crops and precision agriculture.
• Population is projected to plateau near 10 billion, not explode — demographic transition is reducing growth in many countries.
• Innovations like drip irrigation, vertical farming and lab-grown meat suggest more solutions are coming.
Arguments supporting Malthus:
• Around 750 million people remain undernourished — demand is outrunning local food supply in places like Yemen and the Sahel.
• The Aral Sea collapse, depleted aquifers in northern China and the western US, and overfishing in the North Atlantic show resource limits.
• Climate change is already reducing yields in tropical regions, suggesting innovation may not keep pace.
Mastering (7-8): balanced examination, specific evidence on both sides, reasoned conclusion (e.g. Boserup is correct globally, Malthus regionally). [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both theories examined with some specific evidence and a conclusion. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one theory examined more thoroughly, limited evidence. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): theories described not examined, no clear conclusion. [1-2]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT needed for a tropical cyclone to form?
A) Sea surface temperature above 26.5°C
B) Position at least 5° from the equator
C) Cold polar air mass colliding with warm tropical air
D) Low atmospheric wind shear
practice_questions.marks: C) Cold polar air mass colliding with warm tropical air. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'storm surge'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A wall of seawater pushed onto the coast by a tropical cyclone's low pressure and strong onshore winds.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Sea level rising suddenly because of a storm.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern of tropical cyclone tracks.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Form between roughly 5°–25° latitude in summer/autumn over warm tropical oceans (Atlantic, W. Pacific, Indian Ocean).
• Move westwards under the trade winds, then curve polewards.
• Decay over land or over cooler water (above 30° latitude).
Mastering: pattern with latitude band and curved tracks. [3]
Secure: identifies tropical formation and one feature of track. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain why some countries are more vulnerable to tropical cyclones than others.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Physical: low-lying densely populated coasts (Bangladesh delta, Pacific atolls) flood easily; mountainous islands suffer landslides.
• Social: poorer communities live in flimsy housing or informal settlements with no protection; warnings reach remote villages later.
• Economic: developing countries cannot afford sea walls, satellites or robust building codes; recovery depends on aid.
Mastering: linked physical, social AND economic factors with examples. [4]
Secure: two factors developed. [3]
Developing: identifies one factor. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Hurricane Katrina caused 1,800 deaths and Cyclone Nargis caused 138,000 deaths.
Calculate how many times more deaths Cyclone Nargis caused than Hurricane Katrina. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 138,000 ÷ 1,800 = 76.67 times (accept 76–77). Working clear. [4]
Secure: 76 or 77 with method shown. [3]
Developing: division attempted but arithmetic error. [2]
Emerging: tries subtraction or wrong operation. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the effectiveness of methods used to prepare for and respond to tropical cyclones in a developed country and in a developing or emerging country.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Developed country (USA, Hurricane Sandy 2012 or Florida): satellite tracking via the National Hurricane Center, mandatory evacuation orders, federal disaster funding through FEMA, building codes that require storm-resistant construction. Effectiveness: deaths often kept low (Sandy ~160 in the USA), but rebuilding costs huge ($70 bn).
• Developing/emerging country (Bangladesh, since 1970): cyclone shelter network of over 12,000 raised concrete buildings, mass evacuation drills, mobile-phone warnings. Death tolls have fallen from over 300,000 (1970) to under 5,000 in similar storms.
• Differences: developed countries have wealth and technology but coastal property is concentrated and very high-value; developing countries have built community-based systems out of necessity, sometimes with better mortality outcomes.
• Limits: even rich countries fail (Katrina 2005, levees gave way); even prepared developing nations face climate change increasing storm frequency.
Mastering (7–8): nuanced comparison naming cases on both sides with effectiveness measures.
Secure (5–6): clear examples of each, comparison of two methods.
Developing (3–4): basic comparison without specifics.
Emerging (1–2): generalisations without examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a direct threat to tropical rainforests?
A) Climate change causing drought
B) Cattle ranching expansion in Brazil
C) Atmospheric CO2 rising globally
D) Increasing world population
practice_questions.marks: B) Cattle ranching expansion in Brazil. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'nutrient cycle'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The continuous movement of nutrients between living plants, animals, leaf litter and soil within an ecosystem, where decomposition releases nutrients that are reabsorbed by plant roots.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'How nutrients move between plants, animals and soil.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two adaptations that allow rainforest trees to survive in hot, wet conditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Drip-tip leaves shed heavy rain quickly so fungus does not grow on the leaf surface, keeping photosynthesis efficient.
• Buttress roots flare out from the trunk to stabilise tall trees in the shallow forest soil.
• Tall, straight trunks reach light at the canopy level.
• Smooth bark allows climbing plants and rainwater to slide off easily.
Mastering: two adaptations clearly described with explanation of purpose. [3]
Secure: two adaptations named with brief explanation. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how climate change acts as an indirect threat to tropical rainforests.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Higher temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns cause ecosystem stress: trees grow more slowly and shed leaves earlier.
• Drought makes the forest dry enough to burn — Amazon droughts in 2005, 2010 and 2015–16 led to widespread fires.
• Pests and diseases spread further as warmer climates allow them to survive in places they could not before.
• If around 25% of the Amazon is lost, scientists warn of a tipping point where the forest releases more carbon than it absorbs.
Mastering: clear chain of cause and effect with named example (e.g. 2010 Amazon drought). [4]
Secure: two effects explained with reference to climate. [3]

practice_questions.text: A satellite image shows that 18,000 km² of Amazon rainforest was cleared in one year, while in the previous year 10,000 km² was cleared. Calculate the percentage increase. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = 18,000 − 10,000 = 8,000 km²; percentage increase = (8,000 ÷ 10,000) × 100 = 80%. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 80% with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the threats to tropical rainforests, considering both direct and indirect causes of damage.
(8 marks)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Direct threats:
• Commercial agriculture (cattle ranching, soya, palm oil) is the largest cause; Brazilian Amazon clearance is mostly driven by beef and soy exports.
• Hardwood logging removes mahogany and teak, often illegally.
• Mining (iron ore in Carajás, gold in Yanomami territory) strips land and pollutes rivers.
• HEP dams like Belo Monte flood large areas and require new roads, which open further forest to settlers.
• Subsistence farming using slash-and-burn clears smaller patches and uses up nutrients.
Indirect threats:
• Climate change causes drought, ecosystem stress and wildfires (Amazon 2005, 2010, 2015–16).
• Pests and diseases spread further into stressed forests.
• Demand-side pressure: rich-country consumers create export demand for beef, soya and palm oil.
Mastering (7-8): both direct and indirect threats examined with named examples and a clear judgement on which is more serious or how they interact. [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both types covered with examples but limited evaluation. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one type fully covered, other only mentioned. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): description rather than examination, no examples. [1-2]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of soft engineering?
A) A concrete sea wall
B) Rock armour at the cliff base
C) Beach replenishment with offshore sand
D) Wooden groynes at right angles to the shore
practice_questions.marks: C) Beach replenishment with offshore sand. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'strategic realignment'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Deliberately allowing the coast to retreat by breaching or moving back existing sea defences, often creating salt marshes that absorb wave energy and provide habitat.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Letting the sea flood land that used to be defended.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why coastal flood risk is increasing in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Rising sea levels (about 17 cm since 1900) caused by melting ice and ocean thermal expansion.
• More frequent and powerful storms producing larger storm surges.
• Continued building on or near the coast putting more property in harm's way.
Mastering: two reasons with detail. [3]
Secure: two reasons named. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the use of groynes can both protect and harm coastlines.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Process: groynes are wooden or rock fences built at right angles to the shore that trap sand moving by longshore drift.
• Protection: a wider beach absorbs wave energy and protects the cliffs and property behind.
• Harm: sediment is intercepted, so coastline downdrift is starved of beach and erodes faster.
• Named example: Mappleton (Holderness) groynes installed 1991 protected the village but accelerated erosion at Cowden and Aldbrough to the south.
Mastering: protection AND harm explained with named example. [4]
Secure: one side covered well. [2-3]

practice_questions.text: Bournemouth replenishes its beach every 5 years at a cost of £3 million per kilometre. Calculate the total cost over 30 years to maintain a 5 km beach. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 replenishments. 5 km × £3m = £15m per replenishment. 6 × £15m = £90 million total. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: correct answer with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error, method correct. [2]
Emerging: answer only without working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Assess the costs and benefits of hard, soft and sustainable approaches to coastal management at one named UK location.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include (Holderness or Medmerry):
• Hard engineering: Mappleton rock groynes and revetment (1991, £2 million) protect 50 cliff-top properties — sea wall and groynes block erosion but interrupt sediment supply, accelerating loss of land at Cowden and Aldbrough downdrift.
• Soft engineering: Bournemouth beach replenishment costs around £3 million per kilometre every 5 years but absorbs wave energy and supports tourism — must be repeated, sediment supply may be limited.
• Sustainable approaches: Medmerry Managed Realignment (2013) breached the sea wall, flooded 183 hectares of farmland, now protects 348 homes and is an RSPB reserve — saves money and creates habitat, but loses farmland and is unpopular with displaced landowners.
• Conflict: residents of Happisburgh wanted defences but were refused on cost-benefit grounds.
• Conclusion: a mix of approaches, coordinated through Integrated Coastal Zone Management, is increasingly seen as the best way to balance protection, environment and cost.
Mastering (7–8): all three approaches with named examples and clear evaluation.
Secure (5–6): two approaches with examples.
Developing (3–4): one approach covered well.
Emerging (1–2): vague description with no examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a convergent plate boundary?
A) Two plates pulling apart, with magma rising in between
B) Two plates sliding past each other horizontally
C) Two plates moving towards each other, often with subduction
D) An isolated mantle plume below a moving plate
practice_questions.marks: C) Two plates moving towards each other, often with subduction. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'asthenosphere'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The hot, partially molten upper layer of the mantle on which tectonic plates slide.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'A soft layer below the plates.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the global distribution of volcanoes.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Cluster around the edges of the Pacific plate (Pacific Ring of Fire).
• Run along mid-ocean ridges, especially the Mid-Atlantic Ridge through Iceland.
• A few isolated examples sit over hotspots far from plate margins (Hawaii, Yellowstone).
Mastering: pattern with named locations. [3]
Secure: identifies plate boundary clustering plus one example. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain why earthquakes occur at conservative plate boundaries.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Plates slide past each other but not smoothly — friction locks them in place.
• Stress builds up over years or decades as plates continue to push.
• When stress exceeds friction, the plates suddenly slip and the stored energy is released as seismic waves — an earthquake.
• Example: the San Andreas Fault, where the Pacific and North American plates grind past each other.
Mastering: full chain stress build-up → slip → seismic release with example. [4]

practice_questions.text:
An earthquake of magnitude 6 releases roughly 32 times the energy of a magnitude 5.
If magnitude 5 = 8 × 10¹² joules, calculate the energy released by a magnitude 6 quake. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 8 × 10¹² × 32 = 256 × 10¹² = 2.56 × 10¹⁴ J (accept either form). Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: correct method, minor arithmetic error. [3]
Developing: correct multiplication but wrong index notation. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the primary and secondary impacts of an earthquake or volcanic eruption in one developed country and in one developing or emerging country.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Developed country example (Japan, 2011 Tōhoku quake): primary — buildings shaken, transport disrupted, ~18,000 deaths from tsunami; secondary — Fukushima nuclear meltdown, $235 bn economic cost, long-term displacement, food contamination.
• Developing/emerging country example (Haiti, 2010 quake): primary — ~230,000 deaths, capital city collapsed, government paralysed; secondary — cholera outbreak (10,000+ deaths), economic collapse, slow rebuilding.
• Contrast: developed countries suffer huge financial costs but lower death tolls (better building codes, emergency response). Developing countries lose more lives because of unenforced codes, weaker emergency systems and less recovery capacity.
• Both: secondary impacts (disease, economic loss, displacement) often last longer than the primary disaster.
Mastering (7–8): named cases on both sides, primary AND secondary impacts, comparison.
Secure (5–6): two cases, mostly primary impacts, some comparison.
Developing (3–4): one case in detail.
Emerging (1–2): generic statements without specifics.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT a typical adaptation of taiga trees?
A) Needle-shaped leaves
B) Cone-shaped crown
C) Buttress roots
D) Waxy leaf coating
practice_questions.marks: C) Buttress roots. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'permafrost'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Ground that remains frozen throughout the year, with only the top thin active layer thawing during the short summer.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Ground that stays frozen.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways that taiga animals are adapted to long, cold winters.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Some animals (brown bears, ground squirrels) hibernate through winter, living off body fat.
• Many birds and caribou migrate south for winter, returning in spring.
• Year-round residents (lynx, snowshoe hare) grow thick fur or feathers and switch to white coats for camouflage in snow.
• Some store food during the brief summer (squirrels caching pine cones).
Mastering: two adaptations clearly described, with reason. [3]
Secure: two adaptations named with brief explanation. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how acid precipitation damages taiga ecosystems.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Acid rain forms when sulphur and nitrogen oxides from coal-burning and smelting mix with water in the atmosphere.
• When it falls on the taiga it lowers soil pH, killing soil bacteria and damaging fine roots, so trees absorb fewer nutrients.
• Acidic water enters lakes and streams, killing fish eggs and disrupting food chains.
• Around the Sudbury nickel smelter in Ontario, thousands of square kilometres of forest died before pollution controls were tightened.
Mastering: clear cause-effect chain with named example (Sudbury). [4]
Secure: two effects explained. [3]

practice_questions.text: A taiga forest reserve covers 60,000 km². Wildfire destroyed 9,000 km² in one summer. Calculate the percentage of the reserve lost. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: percentage = (9,000 ÷ 60,000) × 100 = 15%. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 15% with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the threats facing the taiga today, considering both commercial development and climate-related factors.
(8 marks)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Commercial development:
• Softwood logging for paper pulp and construction (Russia, Canada, Sweden).
• Fossil fuel extraction — Alberta tar sands clear forest to mine bitumen; Russian Yamal Peninsula gas pipelines.
• Mining for nickel, copper and gold scars and pollutes the landscape.
• HEP dams in Quebec and Russia flood tens of thousands of square kilometres.
Climate-related factors:
• Acid precipitation has killed forest around Sudbury, Ontario.
• Mountain pine beetle outbreaks in British Columbia killed half the merchantable lodgepole pine since the 1990s.
• Russian taiga wildfires in 2019 burned an area the size of Belgium, releasing stored carbon and worsening warming.
• Permafrost thaw threatens long-term carbon storage.
Mastering (7-8): both categories examined with named examples and a reasoned conclusion (e.g. fires and pests now match logging in scale). [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both categories covered with examples but limited evaluation. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one category covered well, other mentioned. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): description rather than examination. [1-2]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a process of river erosion?
A) Saltation
B) Hydraulic action
C) Suspension
D) Deposition
practice_questions.marks: B) Hydraulic action. (Saltation and suspension are transport processes; deposition is the opposite of erosion.) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'meander'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A bend or curve in the middle or lower course of a river formed by lateral erosion shaping the channel sideways.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'A bend in a river.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways a river transports its load.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include: traction (large rocks rolled along bed); saltation (small pebbles bounce); suspension (fine clay/silt carried in water column); solution (dissolved minerals). Mastering: two clearly described. [3]
Secure: two named with brief description. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a waterfall forms in the upper course of a river.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: hard rock band sits above softer rock; water erodes the soft rock by hydraulic action and abrasion; the soft rock undercuts and the hard lip is unsupported; eventually the lip collapses and the waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a gorge behind. Named example: High Force, River Tees. Mastering: full chain of process with named example. [4]

practice_questions.text: A river's discharge rises from 20 m³/s before a storm to a peak of 150 m³/s. Calculate the percentage increase. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = 130; (130 ÷ 20) × 100 = 650%. Working clear, units. [4]
Secure: 650% with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Explain how the landforms found along a river change from the upper to the lower course.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: upper course — steep gradient, vertical erosion dominant; V-shaped valleys, interlocking spurs, waterfalls and gorges (High Force on River Tees). Middle course — gentler gradient, lateral erosion takes over; meanders form, slip-off slopes and river cliffs; ox-bow lakes when meanders cut off. Lower course — wide flat valley; floodplains build up from silt deposition; levees raise channel; deltas at the mouth (Nile, Mississippi). Conclusion: changes reflect declining gradient and increasing discharge as the river matures. Mastering (7–8): all three courses described with named landforms and examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Human Development Index (HDI)?
A) A measure of total income earned in a country
B) A composite of income, education and life expectancy on a 0–1 scale
C) A measure of income inequality
D) The percentage of adults who can read and write
practice_questions.marks: B) A composite of income, education and life expectancy on a 0–1 scale. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two limitations of GDP per capita as a measure of development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: any two of: ignores income inequality; ignores informal economy; ignores quality of life; ignores environmental costs; can be skewed by wealthy elite. [2 marks]
Secure: one valid limitation. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a population pyramid for a developed country differs from one for a developing country.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include: developed has narrow base, wider middle/top, column shape; developing has wide base, narrow top, triangle shape; developed has many over 65, developing few. Mastering: contrast in 3 features. [3]
Secure: contrast in 2. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain why two countries can have similar GDP per capita but very different levels of development.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: income inequality (Gini); public services (Cuba's lower GDP but higher life expectancy than peers); informal economy underestimation; environmental and political conditions. Mastering: 2+ factors with country examples. [4]

practice_questions.text: Niger's HDI is 0.4 and Norway's HDI is 0.96. Calculate the percentage difference between them, taking Niger as the base. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: difference = 0.56; (0.56 ÷ 0.4) × 100 = 140%. Working clear. [4]
Secure: 140% with method, small slip. [3]
Developing: correct method, wrong base. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the strengths and weaknesses of using HDI to compare the development of countries.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: strengths — combines income/education/health; updated yearly; allows ranking. Weaknesses — ignores inequality; ignores environmental sustainability; ignores political freedoms (Saudi Arabia high HDI despite restrictions). Modifications: IHDI corrects for inequality. Conclusion: useful headline measure but should be paired with Gini and political-freedom data. Mastering (7–8): balanced argument with named country examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the main purpose of CITES?
A) To pay countries to plant new forests
B) To regulate the international trade in endangered plant and animal species
C) To certify wood products as sustainable
D) To organise rainforest ecotourism trips
practice_questions.marks: B) To regulate the international trade in endangered plant and animal species. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ecotourism'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Tourism that focuses on undisturbed natural areas and is designed to be low-impact, with money raised funding conservation and local livelihoods.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Tourism in natural areas that helps protect them.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways a forest can be managed sustainably.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Selective logging — only mature trees of certain species are cut, leaving the rest of the canopy intact for regeneration.
• Replanting with native species rather than monoculture plantations to restore ecological function.
• FSC certification — independent verification that a forest is managed to strict environmental and social standards.
• Longer rotation cycles in the taiga (80–120 years) leaving wildlife corridors.
Mastering: two strategies clearly described. [3]
Secure: two strategies named with brief explanation. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Brazilian soy moratorium reduced deforestation in the Amazon.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• In 2006, the largest grain traders agreed not to buy soya beans from any Amazon land cleared after a fixed cut-off date.
• Satellite monitoring and farm registration made it possible to track which farms had cleared forest illegally.
• Supermarkets and consumers pressured traders, lining up market demand with conservation rules.
• Result: soya planted on newly cleared Amazon forest fell from about 30% of new soya area to about 1% by 2014.
Mastering: clear cause-effect chain with quantified outcome. [4]
Secure: process explained with one piece of data. [3]

practice_questions.text: Costa Rica's forest cover rose from 26% of the country in the 1980s to 52% today. Calculate the percentage point increase. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = 52 − 26 = 26 percentage points. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 26 with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the view that global agreements like CITES and REDD have been more effective than local actions in protecting forests.
(8 marks)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Arguments supporting global agreements:
• CITES has cut trade in endangered species; the global ivory ban reduced elephant poaching sharply in some countries.
• REDD payments helped Brazil reduce Amazon deforestation by 80% between 2004 and 2012, with Norwegian funding.
• International rules can pressure governments and TNCs that local communities cannot.
Arguments supporting local actions:
• Indigenous-managed forests show lower clearance rates than many national parks.
• The Brazilian soy moratorium — a market-led local agreement — cut soya planted on newly cleared land from about 30% of new soya area to about 1%.
• Costa Rica's national tree-cover policy and ecotourism raised forest cover from 26% to over 50%.
• Local FSC-certified forestry and Sami land claims show that strong local action protects specific places effectively.
Mastering (7-8): both global and local examined with named examples and a balanced judgement (e.g. global agreements work best when paired with local enforcement). [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both covered with examples but limited evaluation. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one covered well, other only mentioned. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): description rather than examination. [1-2]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of soft engineering for flood management?
A) A concrete flood wall along a riverbank
B) Re-meandering a straightened river
C) A steel flood barrier across a tidal river
D) Channel straightening through a town centre
practice_questions.marks: B) Re-meandering a straightened river. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'lag time' as used on a storm hydrograph.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The time delay between peak rainfall and peak river discharge during a storm.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'The time between rain and the river rising.' [1 mark]
Developing: vague reference to time. [0–1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways that urbanisation increases the risk of river flooding.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Replacement of fields by impermeable concrete and tarmac increases surface runoff.
• Storm drains carry rainfall directly to rivers, shortening lag time.
• Removal of vegetation reduces interception and infiltration.
• Building on the floodplain places more property at risk.
Mastering: two ways with specific mechanism. [3]
Secure: two ways named. [2]
Developing: one way. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how antecedent conditions and basin shape can together produce a flashy hydrograph.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Saturated ground from previous rainfall reduces infiltration so new rain becomes surface runoff almost immediately.
• A round, compact basin concentrates runoff at the outlet at similar times, producing a sharp peak.
• Combined: saturated round basin → fast runoff arriving simultaneously → steep rising limb and short lag.
Mastering: links both factors with a chain of reasoning. [4]
Secure: both factors named with separate explanation. [3]

practice_questions.text: A river had peak rainfall of 30 mm at hour 2 and peak discharge of 120 cumecs at hour 6. Calculate the lag time and state what it suggests about the basin.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: lag time = 6 − 2 = 4 hours [2]; suggests a moderately fast response, possibly impermeable rock or some urban surfaces but not an extreme flashy basin [2]. [4]
Secure: lag time correct, brief interpretation. [3]
Developing: lag time correct only. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the costs and benefits of hard and soft engineering as approaches to managing river flooding. Refer to a UK example in your answer.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Hard engineering benefits: immediate effective protection (Foss Barrier protects c.1,800 York homes); reliable for high-value urban areas.
• Hard engineering costs: high upfront and maintenance cost (Foss Barrier upgrade c.£38m); damages river ecology; can shift the flood problem downstream as faster water moves through.
• Soft engineering benefits: cheaper, sustainable, improves habitats, downstream benefits (Slow the Flow scheme on the upper Calder reduces peak flows downstream).
• Soft engineering costs: requires lots of land that may be in private ownership; slower-acting; may be insufficient for very large floods.
• Named UK example required: River Calder/Hebden Bridge 2015 floods following Storm Eva — c.500 homes flooded; combined approach since.
• Conclusion: most effective plans combine both — hard engineering protects dense urban cores, soft engineering reduces flood peaks across the catchment.
Mastering (7–8): both approaches with strengths AND weaknesses, named UK example, justified judgement.
Secure (5–6): both approaches with example, less balance.
Developing (3–4): one approach in detail.
Emerging (1–2): vague.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a recyclable energy resource?
A) Natural gas
B) Wind power
C) Coal
D) Nuclear fuel
practice_questions.marks: D) Nuclear fuel. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'energy security'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A condition where a country has reliable, affordable and sufficient energy supplies, ideally with a diversified mix of sources to reduce vulnerability to disruption.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Having enough energy supply for a country.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why per-capita energy use varies between countries.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Economic development: wealthier countries have more cars, larger homes, more appliances and heavy industry, all of which raise energy use.
• Reliance on traditional fuels: in poorer countries, many households still cook with wood or charcoal which is only loosely measured.
• Sectoral mix: countries with energy-intensive industries (steel, aluminium, cement) use more energy per unit of GDP than service-led economies.
• Climate: cold countries use more for heating, hot countries for air conditioning.
Mastering: two clear reasons with country examples. [3]
Secure: two reasons named with brief explanation. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how political conflict can affect oil supply and prices.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Conflicts in oil-producing regions cut supply: the 1973 Arab oil embargo restricted exports to the West and quadrupled prices in months.
• Wars disrupt shipping routes: 1990 Gulf War, 2003 Iraq invasion and 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine all caused price spikes.
• Sanctions on oil exporters (e.g. Russia after 2022) force buyers to pay more elsewhere.
• OPEC countries can also choose to cut production for political reasons.
Mastering: clear cause-effect chain with specific dates and named events. [4]
Secure: two effects explained with one named event. [3]

practice_questions.text: An oil price graph shows that oil rose from $40 a barrel in early 2008 to $147 a barrel by July, then fell back to $40 by December. Calculate the percentage increase from January to July. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = $147 − $40 = $107; percentage increase = ($107 ÷ $40) × 100 = 267.5%. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: 267.5% with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error or partial method. [2]
Emerging: answer alone with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the view that the unequal distribution of energy resources causes greater problems than the environmental costs of energy use.
(8 marks)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
Problems from unequal distribution:
• Importing countries (UK, Japan, Germany) face energy insecurity when supplies are disrupted.
• OPEC and Russia can use oil and gas as political leverage; Russia cut gas to Europe in 2022.
• Conflict in oil regions destabilises whole economies (1973 embargo, 2022 Ukraine invasion).
• Poorer importers pay highest share of GDP on energy bills.
Problems from environmental costs:
• Burning fossil fuels emits CO2, the main driver of climate change.
• Oil spills (Deepwater Horizon 2010) damage ecosystems for years.
• Mining and drilling scar landscapes and pollute water (Appalachian coal, Niger Delta oil).
• HEP dams flood communities (Three Gorges displaced 1.3 million people).
Mastering (7-8): both sides examined with named examples and a clear judgement (e.g. distribution causes short-term crises, environmental costs cause long-term harm). [7-8]
Secure (5-6): both covered with examples but limited evaluation. [5-6]
Developing (3-4): one side covered well, other only mentioned. [3-4]
Emerging (1-2): description rather than examination. [1-2]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes the UK's 'urban core'?
A) The most economically active and densely populated region
B) The remote rural areas with the smallest populations
C) The UK's national parks
D) Coastal towns with declining tourism
practice_questions.marks: A) The most economically active and densely populated region. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which UK or EU government policy has tried to reduce differences between the urban core and rural periphery.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: any two of: Enterprise Zones; transport investment such as HS2 or Crossrail; EU Structural Funds; UK Shared Prosperity / Levelling Up Fund; regional development grants. [2]
Secure: one example named clearly. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two changes in the structure of the UK's economy over the past 50 years.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Decline of primary sector employment (mining, fishing, farming) to under 5%.
• Decline of secondary (manufacturing) employment to roughly 10%.
• Rise of tertiary sector (services) to around 75%.
• Rise of quaternary sector (research, IT, biotech) as the fastest-growing area.
Mastering: two changes with figures or named industries. [3]

practice_questions.text: Explain how international migration has changed the population geography of UK cities.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Cities have become more ethnically and culturally diverse — London is around 40% foreign-born in some boroughs.
• Migration boosts the working-age population, partly offsetting the UK's ageing population.
• Migrants cluster in particular neighbourhoods (e.g. Polish in Boston, Bangladeshi in Tower Hamlets), shaping high streets, places of worship and schools.
• Cities outside the South East have also been transformed (Birmingham, Bradford, Leicester).
Mastering: chain of reasoning with named cities and groups. [4]

practice_questions.text: Foreign direct investment (FDI) in the UK was £100 billion in one year. If 40% came from EU countries, how much came from non-EU countries? Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 40% × £100bn = £40bn from EU [1]; £100bn − £40bn = £60bn from non-EU countries [2]; clear method and units stated [1]. [4]
Secure: £60bn correct, method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic correct, no working. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Assess the impact of globalisation and free-trade policies on the UK economy. Refer to TNCs and FDI in your answer.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Free-trade policies and privatisation since 1980s opened the UK to foreign investment.
• TNCs have brought jobs and technology — Nissan in Sunderland (employing around 6,000), JLR's Indian Tata Motors ownership, Toyota at Burnaston.
• FDI has averaged £100bn/year, making the UK one of the world's largest investment destinations.
• Risks: profits return overseas; sudden withdrawal can devastate communities (Honda's Swindon closure announced 2019, Tata Steel reductions in Port Talbot 2024).
• Decline of older industries — UK shed steel, mining and shipbuilding jobs as cheaper foreign producers competed (Consett 1980, Wearside shipyards by 1988).
• Mixed regional outcomes — South East thrived from finance and services, the North East and Wales lost industries; new investment is uneven.
• Conclusion: globalisation has on balance grown the UK economy, but spread the gains unevenly.
Mastering (7–8): balanced view with named TNCs/FDI examples and judgement.
Secure (5–6): mainly one-sided with examples.
Developing (3–4): vague generalisations with one example.
Emerging (1–2): minimal.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of bottom-up, intermediate-technology development?
A) China's Three Gorges Dam
B) A solar-lantern programme run by an NGO in rural Kenya
C) A motorway built by a national government
D) A new international airport
practice_questions.marks: B) A solar-lantern programme run by an NGO in rural Kenya. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'transnational corporation (TNC)'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A company that operates in two or more countries, with offices, factories or shops in multiple nations.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'A big company that works in lots of countries.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of intermediate technology.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Low cost — affordable for poor communities.
• Locally repairable — communities can maintain it without specialists.
• Suited to existing skill levels and resources of the population.
• Sustainable — uses renewable energy or local materials.
Mastering: two characteristics with explanation. [3]
Secure: two characteristics named. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how TNCs can both help and harm a developing country.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Help: bring foreign direct investment, create jobs, transfer skills and technology, raise tax revenues, push up wages over time.
• Harm: profits often returned home not reinvested locally; can pay low wages or use poor working conditions; multiple-country accounting can avoid corporation tax; environmental harm in countries with weak regulation.
• Specific: Apple manufacturing in China lifted Foxconn workers' wages but came under criticism for working hours and environment.
Mastering: balanced 'help and harm' with named example. [4]

practice_questions.text: A new TNC factory in Vietnam pays 200 workers $300/month each. How much extra wage income enters the local economy each year? Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: monthly = 200 × $300 = $60,000; annual = $60,000 × 12 = $720,000. Working clear and units stated. [4]
Secure: $720,000 with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error, method correct. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the advantages and disadvantages of top-down and bottom-up approaches to development.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Top-down advantages: scale (Three Gorges Dam now provides 22.5 GW of electricity to China); speed (large infrastructure built in years not decades); national-level economic growth.
• Top-down disadvantages: cost (Three Gorges cost tens of billions of dollars, funded by Chinese state banks after the World Bank refused to back it); displacement (1.3 million people relocated); environmental damage (loss of habitats, sediment build-up).
• Bottom-up advantages: appropriate to need (Practical Action solar-drip irrigation in Zimbabwe doubled smallholder yields cheaply); locally owned and sustainable; few people displaced.
• Bottom-up disadvantages: small scale (cannot replace a national grid); patchy funding from charity; cannot deliver national infrastructure.
• Conclusion: real development needs both — large infrastructure for grids, ports and rail; community-scale work for clean water, agriculture and health.
Mastering (7–8): both approaches with strengths AND weaknesses, named examples.
Secure (5–6): both approaches with examples, less balance.
Developing (3–4): one approach in detail.
Emerging (1–2): vague.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an unconventional fossil fuel?
A) Natural gas from a conventional well
B) Shale gas extracted by fracking
C) Onshore wind power
D) Solar photovoltaic
practice_questions.marks: B) Shale gas extracted by fracking. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define 'carbon footprint'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The total amount of greenhouse gases emitted directly or indirectly by an individual, organisation or activity.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'How much CO₂ a person or company produces.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways individuals can reduce their carbon footprint.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: cut meat consumption; choose low-carbon transport (cycle, train, electric car); fewer or no flights; insulate homes; switch electricity supplier to renewable tariff; reduce consumption of fast fashion. Mastering: two specific actions. [3]

practice_questions.text: Explain why developing fossil-fuel resources in ecologically sensitive areas (e.g. tar sands, Arctic oil) is controversial.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: high CO₂ intensity (tar sands 3× conventional); damage to fragile habitats and Indigenous lands; risk of oil spills in harsh remote conditions; locks in fossil-fuel use just as transition is needed; benefits flow to TNCs and governments not to local people. Mastering: 2+ reasons developed. [4]

practice_questions.text: If global solar PV costs fell 90% from 2010 to 2024, and a 1 kW system cost $7,500 in 2010, calculate the 2024 cost. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 90% decrease means new price = 10% of $7,500 = $750. Working clear, units. [4]
Secure: $750 with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the costs and benefits of switching from fossil fuels to renewable energy in a developed country.
(8 marks)
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: benefits — cuts CO₂ emissions; reduces import dependence (UK gas was 50% from Norway in 2022); creates new jobs (UK offshore wind sector now employs 30,000+); improves air quality. Costs — high upfront capital; intermittency requires storage; fossil-fuel jobs lost; some communities oppose wind farms; rare metals for batteries cause new environmental issues. Conclusion: long-run benefits outweigh short-term costs but transition must be planned with affected workers. Mastering (7–8): both costs and benefits, named examples and figures.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the largest sector of India's economy today?
A) Agriculture
B) Manufacturing
C) Services
D) Mining
practice_questions.marks: C) Services. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why India is a favourable location for foreign direct investment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: any two of: large English-speaking workforce; coastal access via Indian Ocean ports; large domestic market (1.4 bn people); 1991 liberalisation policies; 'Make in India' incentives; democratic government; growing middle class. [2 marks]
Secure: one reason. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the changing structure of India's economy since 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Decline of agriculture as a share of GDP from ~30% (1990) to ~18% (today).
• Rise of services from a smaller share to ~50% of GDP, dominated by IT and business services.
• Industry around 25%, with manufacturing growing through 'Make in India'.
Mastering: figures and trend across all three sectors. [3]
Secure: shift between two sectors with rough figures. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how globalisation has driven India's economic development.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• 1991 liberalisation reduced tariffs and welcomed FDI, attracting TNCs that brought capital, skills and technology.
• Cheap mobile and internet connectivity, plus an English-speaking workforce, allowed India to become the world's back-office and software services hub (Bengaluru, Hyderabad).
• TNCs like Apple now manufacture in India (Tamil Nadu) for export; Infosys and TCS sell IT services to global clients.
• Result: GDP growth of ~7% per year, lifting 415 million people out of poverty.
Mastering: causal chain liberalisation → FDI → sector growth → poverty reduction. [4]

practice_questions.text:
If India's GDP grew at an average of 7% per year for 10 years, by what factor has it grown?
(Use the formula 1.07¹⁰ ≈ 1.97). Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 1.07¹⁰ ≈ 1.97, so GDP nearly doubled (~97% increase). Working clear. [4]
Secure: states ~2× or 97% with method. [3]
Developing: ~70% (using simple addition not compounding) — partial credit for method. [2]
Emerging: any plausible attempt. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the positive and negative impacts of rapid economic development on people and the environment in India.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Positive — people: ~415 million lifted out of poverty since 2005; middle class now ~350 million; life expectancy up from 41 (1960) to 70; literacy rates rising; women's workforce participation expanding.
• Positive — environment: rapid expansion of solar power (solar capacity up from 82 GW in early 2024 to over 160 GW by 2026); 'Clean India' (Swachh Bharat) sanitation programme; international climate pledges.
• Negative — people: inequality (top 10% take 57% of income); 230 million still in poverty; sharp regional gaps between Mumbai/Bengaluru core and Bihar/UP periphery; informal-sector workers without protection.
• Negative — environment: Delhi PM2.5 routinely 10× WHO limits; Yamuna and Ganges heavily polluted; loss of farmland to sprawl; coal still 70% of electricity.
• Conclusion: Growth has lifted hundreds of millions but at significant cost — sustainability remains a challenge.
Mastering (7–8): four named impacts (2 + 2) with figures.
Secure (5–6): three impacts with examples.
Developing (3–4): general statements, weak figures.
Emerging (1–2): one-sided.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes Birmingham's CBD?
A) The historic farmland on the edge of the city
B) The central commercial and retail district with the highest land values
C) Suburban semi-detached housing
D) The Victorian inner-city terraces
practice_questions.marks: B) The central commercial and retail district with the highest land values. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by the 'situation' of a city, using Birmingham as an example.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A city's location in relation to other places — Birmingham sits centrally in the UK with motorway, rail and canal links to other regions.' [2]
Secure: 'Where a city is in the country' with one example. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which migration has shaped Birmingham's population.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Caribbean migration since 1948 settled in Handsworth and Aston, shaping Birmingham's cultural mix.
• South Asian (especially Pakistani and Bangladeshi) migration concentrated in Sparkbrook and Aston from the 1960s.
• EU migration after 2004 (Polish, Romanian, Bulgarian) added new inner-city populations.
• Birmingham is now around 50% ethnic minority and one of Europe's youngest cities.
Mastering: two ways with named groups and areas. [3]
Secure: two ways named more generally. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how Birmingham's structure produces inequality between different parts of the city.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Land values fall with distance from the CBD, so housing types and quality vary sharply.
• Inner-city Victorian terraces in Sparkbrook house lower-income migrants and former factory workers; deprivation indices are very high.
• Suburbs like Sutton Coldfield are wealthy with detached housing and good schools.
• Health, education and employment outcomes follow housing geography (life expectancy gap of around 7 years).
Mastering: chain of reasoning linking land use, housing, services and outcomes. [4]

practice_questions.text: Birmingham's population grew from 977,000 at the 2001 census to 1,144,000 at the 2021 census. Calculate the percentage increase. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: increase = 1,144,000 − 977,000 = 167,000 [1]; % = (167,000 ÷ 977,000) × 100 = 17.09% (≈ 17.1%) [2]; clear method and units stated [1]. [4]
Secure: ≈17% with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic correct, no working. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Assess the relative importance of site, situation and migration in shaping Birmingham today.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Site: Birmingham Plateau, gently rolling at 150–180 m, no defining river — physical site is unremarkable.
• Situation: central UK, hub of canals (Grand Union, Birmingham), railways (New Street, Curzon Street/HS2), motorways (M6, M5, M40, M42), Birmingham Airport — drives FDI and TNC location.
• Functions: financial and corporate hub (HSBC UK relocated 2018, Deutsche Bank), retail (Bullring, Selfridges), HE (University of Birmingham, Aston), advanced manufacturing legacy.
• Migration: Caribbean (1948 Windrush), South Asian (1960s+), EU (2004+) populations cluster in inner-city wards (Handsworth, Sparkbrook), making Birmingham 50%+ ethnic minority and Europe's youngest big city.
• Structure: classic CBD/inner city/suburbs/fringe model with sharp inequalities — Sparkbrook in the most deprived 10% in England, Sutton Coldfield among the most affluent.
• Conclusion: situation drives functions; migration drives population; site is a minor factor — together they explain modern Birmingham.
Mastering (7–8): all three drivers covered with named facts and judgement.
Secure (5–6): two drivers covered.
Developing (3–4): one driver, vague.
Emerging (1–2): minimal.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct definition of a megacity?
A) A capital city of any country
B) An urban area with more than 1 million people
C) An urban area with more than 10 million people
D) The largest city in a continent
practice_questions.marks: C) An urban area with more than 10 million people. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'urban primacy'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'When one city is far larger and more economically and politically dominant than any other city in the country, often holding much of its population, government and industry.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'When one city dominates a country.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why the urban population of an emerging country might grow rapidly.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Rural-urban migration as people leave farming for factory or service jobs.
• Natural increase — high birth rates among the young migrant population already in cities.
• Industrialisation creating concentrated employment that pulls people in.
• Better access to healthcare, education and electricity in cities than in rural areas.
Mastering: two reasons clearly developed. [3]
Secure: two reasons named. [2]
Developing: one reason given. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how push and pull factors lead to rural-urban migration in a developing country.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Push: rural poverty, drought, mechanised farming reducing jobs, lack of schools or clinics force people to leave the countryside.
• Pull: city offers higher wages, factory jobs, hospitals, schools and electricity.
• Process: young adults move first, find informal-sector work, then send money home or bring family.
• Result: cities grow rapidly through migration plus the natural increase of young migrants having children.
Mastering: linked chain of cause → process → result with named factors. [4]
Secure: push and pull factors stated with some explanation. [2-3]

practice_questions.text: Lagos grew from 7.3 million in 2000 to 15.4 million in 2024. Calculate the percentage increase. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: change = 15.4 − 7.3 = 8.1 million. 8.1 ÷ 7.3 = 1.1096. × 100 = 110.9% (accept 111%). Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: correct answer with method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error but correct method. [2]
Emerging: only the answer given with no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine why urbanisation rates and patterns differ between developed and emerging or developing countries.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Developed countries (e.g. UK, Japan): already 80%+ urban so urbanisation is slow or static; suburbanisation, counter-urbanisation and re-urbanisation are reshaping cities rather than expanding them; jobs are mainly in services.
• Emerging countries (e.g. India, Brazil, China): urban share growing fast, driven by industrialisation; megacities like Mumbai or São Paulo expand into surrounding farmland; mix of formal and informal jobs.
• Developing countries (e.g. Nigeria, Ethiopia): low urban share but the fastest urbanisation rates; Lagos adds approximately 77 people per hour; high natural increase plus large rural-urban migration; informal sector dominates employment; slums grow alongside formal districts.
• Causes of difference: stage of economic development, role of agriculture, government investment in cities, fertility rates, infrastructure capacity.
• Conclusion: the world's centre of urban growth has shifted from Europe and North America (19th–20th century) to Asia and Africa today.
Mastering (7–8): two or more contrasts with named examples and reasons.
Secure (5–6): contrast made with examples, less developed reasoning.
Developing (3–4): one country type covered well, others mentioned.
Emerging (1–2): vague description with no examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of de-centralisation?
A) Building a flagship office tower in the CBD
B) Opening an out-of-town retail park on the urban-rural fringe
C) Demolishing a Victorian terraced street
D) Investing in a city-centre tram line
practice_questions.marks: B) Opening an out-of-town retail park on the urban-rural fringe. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'gentrification' in the context of urban change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The upgrading of inner-city neighbourhoods by higher-income incomers, often raising rents and house prices and changing the character of the area.' [2]
Secure: 'When richer people move into and improve a poorer area.' [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which UK city centres have changed because of e-commerce.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Closure of department stores (Debenhams, House of Fraser) leaving large empty anchor units.
• Rising shop vacancy rates, above 20% in some smaller town centres.
• Reduced footfall and fewer independent shops on high streets.
• Conversion of redundant retail space into housing or leisure uses.
Mastering: two ways with named retailers or data. [3]

practice_questions.text: Explain how flagship regeneration projects can both benefit and harm the surrounding community.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Benefits: new jobs (London Docklands employs over 150,000), modern housing, improved environmental quality, public transport upgrades, prestige.
• Harms: rising rents and house prices displace long-term low-income residents (Hackney average house prices rose from £100k to £600k+); benefits often concentrated in the flagship area, leaving neighbouring communities still deprived.
• Balanced answers note that the best schemes mix tenure types and engage local communities.
Mastering: chain of reasoning with named example covering both benefit and harm. [4]

practice_questions.text: London's ULEZ cut roadside nitrogen dioxide in the central zone by 44%. If pre-ULEZ levels were 80 µg/m³, what is the new level? Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 44% × 80 = 35.2; new level = 80 − 35.2 = 44.8 µg/m³ [3]; method clearly shown with units [1]. [4]
Secure: 44.8 µg/m³ correct, method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic correct without method. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the strategies UK cities use to make urban living more sustainable. Refer to a named example in your answer.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Sustainable transport: London ULEZ cut roadside NO₂ by ~44% in central zones; Birmingham Clean Air Zone; cycle networks.
• Sustainable housing: BedZED Sutton (~100 zero-carbon homes); retrofit programmes; affordable housing schemes in London boroughs.
• Green spaces: Sheffield's 250 woodlands; City of Trees Manchester planting programme; protected greenbelts.
• Recycling: kerbside collection has lifted UK municipal recycling to 44%, but progress has stalled.
• Limits: ULEZ has been politically contested (driver charges); BedZED has not been replicated at scale; recycling rates plateauing.
• Conclusion: best results come from combining transport, housing and green-space strategies — single measures rarely transform a city.
Mastering (7–8): multiple strategies with named examples and data, balanced judgement.
Secure (5–6): two strategies with examples.
Developing (3–4): one strategy or vague.
Emerging (1–2): minimal.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the 12-mark decision question?
A) A short-answer recall question
B) A long-answer essay choosing between options using booklet evidence
C) A calculation question about percentage change
D) A multiple-choice question on definitions
