practice_questions.marks: B) A long-answer essay choosing between options using booklet evidence. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of evidence found in a resources booklet.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: any two of: graphs/charts; maps; photographs; statistical tables; quotes from stakeholders; news extracts. [2 marks]
Secure: one valid type. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the three dimensions you should weigh when comparing options in a decision essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include: economic (cost, jobs, GDP, who pays); environmental (CO₂, biodiversity, pollution, land use); social (people affected, equity, displacement, cultural value). Mastering: all three with brief description. [3]
Secure: two named. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain why identifying stakeholders helps build a strong decision essay.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: stakeholders are different groups affected by the decision (Indigenous peoples, businesses, governments, NGOs); listing them prevents one-sided answers; understanding what each wants reveals trade-offs; lets you address opposing views in your reasoning; demonstrates the balanced thinking the mark scheme rewards. Mastering: 2+ reasons developed. [4]

practice_questions.text: If a logging concession covers 1,200 km² and removes 60% of the forest, calculate the area of forest cleared. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 1,200 × 0.6 = 720 km². Working clear, units. [4]
Secure: 720 km² with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error. [2]
Emerging: tries multiplication, wrong base. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A booklet presents three strategies for managing a tropical rainforest: (1) commercial logging with quotas; (2) full national park protection; (3) ecotourism with selective small-scale logging.
Evaluate which option you would choose, justifying your decision.
(12 marks)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): clear decision with developed reasoning across economic, environmental and social dimensions; cites at least 3 specific booklet sources; addresses the strengths and weaknesses of all three options; explicit comparison in the conclusion explaining why the chosen option is preferable to the alternatives.
Secure (7–9): clear decision with reasoning; addresses 2+ options; cites some booklet evidence; conclusion may not fully explain rejection of alternatives.
Developing (4–6): a decision is stated; reasoning limited to one or two factors; uses some evidence.
Emerging (1–3): a choice is made but with little reasoning or evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes Dharavi?
A) The CBD of Mumbai
B) A new suburb on the urban-rural fringe
C) One of the largest slums in Asia
D) Mumbai's container port
practice_questions.marks: C) One of the largest slums in Asia. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'site' as it applies to a city.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'The actual land or physical area on which a city is built, including its relief, water bodies and ground conditions.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'The land a city stands on.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two challenges that rapid population growth has created for residents of Mumbai.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Housing shortage — about 41% of residents live in slums.
• Insecure property rights — slum dwellers can be evicted with little notice.
• Inadequate water supply — supply for as little as 2–4 hours per day in some areas.
• Traffic congestion costs around 8% of GDP a year.
• Air pollution above WHO safe limits, causing respiratory illness.
Mastering: two challenges with detail/figures. [3]
Secure: two challenges named without detail. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the site and situation of Mumbai have helped it become a global city.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Site: built on seven joined islands forming a long peninsula with a deep natural harbour.
• Harbour: ideal for shipping and now India's busiest container port.
• Situation: faces the Indian Ocean — central to trade routes between Europe, Africa and Asia.
• Connectivity: international airport, suburban rail and undersea data cables tie Mumbai into global finance and IT networks.
• Result: financial centre with stock exchange, RBI and major banks, plus headquarters of TNCs and Bollywood.
Mastering: at least one site point and one situation point linked to global role. [4]
Secure: factors named with limited explanation. [2-3]

practice_questions.text: Mumbai's population was 12 million in 1991 and 18 million in 2011. Calculate the percentage increase. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: change = 18 − 12 = 6 million. 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5. × 100 = 50% increase. Working clear, units stated. [4]
Secure: correct answer with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error, method correct. [2]
Emerging: answer only, no working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the opportunities and challenges facing residents of one named megacity in a developing or emerging country.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include (Mumbai):
• Opportunities: better wages than rural areas (roughly 5× village pay for unskilled work); free public hospitals and government schools; informal entrepreneurship — Dharavi produces around US$1 billion of output annually from small workshops; access to top universities such as IIT Bombay; cultural and sporting opportunities.
• Challenges: housing shortage with 41% of people in slums; insecure property rights leading to forced evictions; intermittent water supply (2–4 hours per day); air pollution above WHO safe limits; traffic congestion costing the city about 8% of GDP per year.
• Inequality: extreme contrast between Antilia (US$2 billion private skyscraper) and adjacent slum housing.
• Causes of contrasts: skill gap rewards English-speaking professionals; land scarcity on a peninsula drives property prices up; politicians struggle to manage as slum dwellers are also voters.
• Conclusion: opportunities and challenges co-exist in the same neighbourhoods; rapid growth has been broadly positive but with serious unresolved inequalities.
Mastering (7–8): both opportunities AND challenges with named places and figures.
Secure (5–6): both covered, fewer specifics.
Developing (3–4): one side covered well.
Emerging (1–2): generic megacity points without examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes counter-urbanisation?
A) People moving from rural areas into cities for jobs
B) People moving out of cities into smaller towns and rural areas
C) People moving between two cities for work
D) Tourists visiting national parks at weekends
practice_questions.marks: B) People moving out of cities into smaller towns and rural areas. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two challenges faced by accessible rural areas in the UK today.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: any two of: unaffordable housing for local young adults; declining primary employment; reduced rural healthcare access; closing village schools; congestion from leisure visitors; loss of village identity. [2]
Secure: one challenge with brief explanation. [1]

practice_questions.text: Describe two flows between cities and accessible rural areas.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Goods: food and timber from rural areas into city markets; manufactured goods and online deliveries from city to rural.
• Services: rural residents travel to city hospitals, universities, large shops and entertainment.
• Labour: commuters travel from villages into city offices; some city residents work in rural distribution centres or tourism.
Mastering: two flows with direction and example. [3]

practice_questions.text: Explain how counter-urbanisation has changed the housing market in accessible rural areas.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Higher demand from incoming commuters and second-home buyers raises house prices.
• Local young adults priced out — Bourton-on-the-Water average prices over £500k vs lower local wages.
• Some councils respond with planning rules (St Ives 2016 second-home ban) or rural exception sites.
• Long-standing rural families displaced or unable to inherit homes; village character changes as full-time residents are replaced by part-timers.
Mastering: chain of reasoning linking cause, effect and policy response. [4]

practice_questions.text: Lake District tourism employs 18,000 people and contributes £1.4 billion to the local economy. Calculate the average contribution per tourism job. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: £1,400,000,000 ÷ 18,000 = £77,777.78 (≈£77,800) per job [3]; method shown with units [1]. [4]
Secure: ≈£78k per job, method shown. [3]
Developing: arithmetic correct, no method or units. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the costs and benefits of interdependence between cities and accessible rural areas. Refer to UK examples in your answer.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Benefits to rural areas: incoming commuter spending; new businesses; expanded services such as broadband and improved roads; tourism revenue (Lake District ~£1.4bn from 18m visitors).
• Benefits to cities: cheaper food, weekend leisure space, labour pool of skilled commuters.
• Costs to rural areas: house-price inflation (Cotswolds, St Ives), strain on schools and surgeries, environmental damage (Helvellyn footpath erosion £1m+ repair), seasonal economies.
• Costs to cities: loss of middle-class residents (counter-urbanisation), congestion at peak times.
• Diversification: farm shops, glamping, dark-sky tourism, sustainable energy projects help spread benefits.
• Conclusion: interdependence has on balance lifted accessible rural areas, but communities have to manage housing affordability and environmental pressure carefully.
Mastering (7–8): balanced view with named UK examples and judgement.
Secure (5–6): mainly one-sided with examples.
Developing (3–4): vague.
Emerging (1–2): minimal.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a bottom-up strategy in Mumbai?
A) The Mumbai Metro
B) The Mumbai Coastal Road
C) SPARC building community toilet blocks
D) The Middle Vaitarna Dam
practice_questions.marks: C) SPARC building community toilet blocks. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sustainable city'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'A city designed to meet the needs of its people today without damaging the environment or the ability of future generations to meet their needs, through clean transport, fair housing and efficient resource use.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'A city that meets needs without harming the future.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two top-down strategies that aim to improve transport in Mumbai.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Mumbai Metro expansion from one line to a planned 14 lines by 2030, designed to move millions off the rail and road networks.
• The Mumbai Coastal Road (opened 2024) cut a one-hour drive to about 20 minutes between south Mumbai and the western suburbs.
• Replacing 1,800 BEST diesel buses with electric vehicles to cut roadside pollution.
• The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link sea bridge to Navi Mumbai opened in 2024.
Mastering: two strategies described with specifics. [3]
Secure: two named without much detail. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain how an NGO-led project can improve sustainability in a megacity.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Project chosen, e.g. SPARC's community toilet blocks in over 250 Mumbai settlements.
• Design suits local needs — locally managed by trained women, low cost, locally repairable.
• Sustainability outcome — reduces open defecation and disease without requiring expensive sewer infrastructure.
• Wider impact — empowers women, creates local jobs, builds community ownership.
• Alternative example acceptable: Stree Mukti recycling cooperatives reducing landfill and giving informal workers ID cards and pay.
Mastering: named NGO project + sustainability outcome explained. [4]
Secure: NGO project mentioned with weaker reasoning. [2-3]

practice_questions.text: Mumbai loses about 30% of its piped water to leaks. If the daily supply is 4,000 million litres, calculate how many litres are lost each day. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 30% of 4,000 = 0.30 × 4,000 = 1,200 million litres per day. Working clearly shown, units stated. [4]
Secure: correct answer with method. [3]
Developing: correct method with arithmetic slip. [2]
Emerging: answer only without working. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Examine the advantages and disadvantages of top-down and bottom-up strategies for making one named megacity in a developing or emerging country more sustainable.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include (Mumbai):
• Top-down advantages: scale (Mumbai Metro will move 12 million passengers a day); speed (large infrastructure built within years); foreign investment (World Bank co-finance); national prestige and visible results.
• Top-down disadvantages: high cost overruns (e.g. Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train delayed); communities sometimes displaced and rehoused in tower blocks that break up neighbourhood networks; slum-rehabilitation tower blocks criticised for inflating developer profits.
• Bottom-up advantages: appropriate to need (SPARC toilet blocks designed and run by local women); little displacement; locally maintainable and locally owned; income for informal workers (Stree Mukti recycling cooperatives organising 250,000 ragpickers).
• Bottom-up disadvantages: small scale (SPARC's 250 settlements are a fraction of slum residents); donor-funded so vulnerable to funding cuts; cannot deliver a Metro line or major water project.
• Conclusion: real sustainability requires both — major infrastructure for water and transport, plus community projects for housing, sanitation and skills. Hybrid models like the Slum Sanitation Programme are most effective.
Mastering (7–8): both approaches with named examples and clear evaluation.
Secure (5–6): both approaches covered with examples, less explicit comparison.
Developing (3–4): one approach covered well.
Emerging (1–2): vague description with no examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the FIRST stage of the geographical enquiry process?
A) Drawing conclusions
B) Formulating questions and hypotheses
C) Selecting fieldwork methods
D) Presenting data
practice_questions.marks: B) Formulating questions and hypotheses. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define 'primary data'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Data collected first-hand by the researcher in the field, such as personal measurements, observations or questionnaires.' [2 marks]
Secure: 'Data you collect yourself.' [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of systematic sampling.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: strength — even coverage; easy to plan; reduces sampler bias. Weakness — may miss important features falling between intervals; not statistically unbiased if there is a hidden pattern at the same interval. Mastering: strength + weakness with specifics. [3]

practice_questions.text: Explain why critical reflection is an important stage of the enquiry process.
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: identifies limitations of the data and method (sample size, weather conditions); suggests improvements for next time; helps interpret confidence in conclusions; demonstrates honest reporting required of all real geographical research. Mastering: 2+ reasons developed with examples. [4]

practice_questions.text:
A river survey measures discharge at six sites. The values are 0.4, 0.7, 1.2, 1.8, 2.4, 3.1 m³/s. Calculate the mean discharge.
Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: total = 9.6; mean = 9.6 ÷ 6 = 1.6 m³/s. Working clear, units. [4]
Secure: 1.6 m³/s with method. [3]
Developing: arithmetic error. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of two methods of presenting fieldwork data.
(8 marks plus 4 SPaG)
practice_questions.marks: Students may include: bar charts strong for comparing categories; weak for showing trends over time. Line graphs strong for continuous data; weak for categorical data. Choropleth maps strong for spatial patterns; weak when classes hide internal variation. Scatter graphs strong for showing correlation; weak when patterns are non-linear. Conclusion: choose method to match data type and audience. Mastering (7–8): two methods, both sides of strengths/weaknesses, named examples.
